claims.text: High-temperature wear resistance of thin FeNiCrCoCu coatings is governed by the formation and stability of a protective, adherent oxide layer.
Thermal exposure forms an oxide layer on the coating surface.
The oxide layer increases local surface hardness.
The oxide layer acts as an intrinsic solid lubricant and lowers friction.
The oxide-mediated increase in hardness and reduction in friction mitigate abrasive and adhesive wear.
An oxide layer that becomes too thick or spalls under excessive thermal exposure causes wear resistance to deteriorate.
The as-sprayed coating has high room-temperature hardness that resists abrasive and fatigue wear.
The as-sprayed FeNiCrCoCu coating has a fine nanostructure.
Annealing at approximately 500°C promotes a coherent protective oxide without excessive grain growth or oxide spallation.
The thermally generated layer is likely composed of Fe, Cr, and Cu oxides.
The thermally generated oxide is nanocrystalline, mechanically robust, and adherent.
A 500°C vacuum heat treatment produces the lowest wear rate and best wear resistance because it produces the highest microhardness.
A coating pretreated at approximately 500°C will have a lower friction coefficient than untreated and 700°C-treated coatings.
A coating pretreated at approximately 500°C will exhibit less wear than the room-temperature untreated condition and higher-temperature-treated conditions.
Heat treatment at 700°C decreases coating hardness, intensifies abrasive wear, and promotes crack-driven peeling.
Treatment at approximately 700°C causes thicker oxide growth and grain coarsening.
Relevant coating wear modes include adhesive, abrasive, fatigue, and oxidation wear.
The proposed mechanism applies to high-temperature sliding between approximately 500°C and 700°C.
The proposed mechanism applies in a simulated high-temperature drilling-fluid environment.
The hypothesis does not apply where chemical corrosion dominates mechanical wear.

contradictions.description: The baseline is defined as an as-sprayed coating tested at room temperature, whereas the conditions and falsification design describe high-temperature testing of the coating set. It is therefore unclear whether the untreated control is tested at room temperature or at the same high temperature as the annealed samples, creating a test-temperature confound.
